Chapter 5: Measuring and Sustaining Engagement—The Role of the Twelve Questions.
Now that we’ve seen just how crucial the manager-employee relationship really is, let’s shift gears and talk about something just as important—how do you actually measure and keep engagement alive over time?
Engagement isn’t some mysterious feeling floating around. It’s a real set of attitudes and behaviors you can spot, measure, and even improve.
Enter the “Twelve Questions.” Think of these as your go-to toolkit for checking the pulse of your team. They’re built on tons of research about what truly drives engagement and performance. These questions dig into the nuts and bolts—everything from whether people know what’s expected of them, to if they feel recognized and have chances to grow.
They’re laid out in a logical order. The basics come first, like clarity and having the right tools. Then we move up to questions about belonging and being recognized, and finally, we get to opportunities for growth and a sense of purpose.
Picture it like a pyramid, each level stacking on the one before. If those basic needs at the bottom aren’t met, it’s tough for someone to reach a sense of belonging, let alone find real purpose at work. Imagine not knowing what’s expected of you—how could you feel you really belong, or see the bigger picture?
Managers can use these questions almost like a regular check-up. It doesn’t have to be formal—sometimes, it’s just about paying attention to the energy in the room or having a quick chat over coffee. But you can also use surveys or scheduled conversations to spot what’s working and what’s not.
So, what does this look like in real life? Here are some practical ways you can put the Twelve Questions to work:
First, make regular check-ins part of your routine. Sit down with each person and talk about how they’re doing and what they need.
Next, use what you learn from engagement surveys to create action plans. Focus on specific steps you can take to make the team’s environment better.
Don’t forget to celebrate progress. Even small wins matter! Recognizing these moments builds momentum and keeps everyone moving in the right direction.
And remember, engagement isn’t a box you check off once and forget about. It’s an ongoing process—a journey, not a destination. Keep looking for new ways to make the workplace better for everyone.
Here’s something to keep in mind: sustaining engagement means staying curious and willing to learn. People’s needs can change. What worked last year—or even last month—might not work now. The best managers are always experimenting, adapting, and listening.
This way of working builds a culture where trust, accountability, and improvement are just part of daily life. When people see that their voices matter and their feedback leads to real action, they’re way more likely to feel engaged and committed. In the long run, that means better performance, less turnover, and a deeper sense of purpose for everyone involved.
So, here’s the key takeaway: measuring and sustaining engagement is about much more than ticking off a checklist. It’s about building a place where people feel valued, supported, and inspired to do their best. The Twelve Questions are a simple, powerful way to make that happen—one honest conversation at a time.
